Operating a two-GPU inference service requires a sophisticated orchestration layer that balances raw computational throughput with the physical constraints of hardware interconnects and memory bandwidth. The foundational challenge lies in scheduling, where the system must dynamically allocate incoming inference requests to the appropriate GPU based on current load, model partitioning strategies, and latency requirements. In a dual-GPU setup, the scheduler often employs a hybrid approach, combining static model sharding for large language models with dynamic request routing for smaller, latency-sensitive tasks. This ensures that neither GPU becomes a bottleneck while the other remains idle, a common failure mode in naive round-robin scheduling schemes that ignore the varying computational costs of different token lengths or batch sizes.

A naive round-robin approach often fails in heterogeneous workloads, so a more intelligent scheduler is necessary to track the queue depth and processing time of each GPU, directing new tasks to the unit with the lowest predicted completion time. This scheduling logic must also account for kernel launch overheads and context switching costs, which can be significant when alternating between different model architectures or batch sizes on the same device.

The core of this operation lies in the compute scheduling strategy, which must dynamically allocate incoming inference requests to the available GPUs based on real-time load metrics, model complexity, and batch size optimization. A naive round-robin approach often fails in heterogeneous workloads, so a more intelligent scheduler is required to monitor queue depths and kernel execution times, directing traffic to the GPU with the lowest predicted latency for the specific request type. This scheduling logic must also account for the overhead of context switching between different models or batch configurations, as frequent switches can degrade performance significantly due to the cost of reloading weights and resetting CUDA contexts.
